rubrics.title: Quick Write 17 — Four Lines of Verse

ratings.long_description: Four to six unrhymed lines of about five beats each that make the rule and the choice clear.
Fewer than four lines, rhymed lines, or a rhythm or conflict that is hard to follow.
Names one deliberate bend, quotes the line, and explains what the bend makes a reader notice.
Names no bend, or says only that the line sounds good.
One inverted line and two Word Study words used accurately; the note is 100 to 150 words.
Fewer than two of either, or off the length target.

rubrics.title: Quick Write 18 — What the Text Specifies

criteria.description: What the text fixes and leaves open

ratings.long_description: Names two fixed features and two open choices, each with a specific example from the scene.
Fixed and open features are mixed up, general, or missing examples.
A clear paragraph connects the scene to the play’s central events or ideas.
The paragraph retells the scene or stays general.
Two prepositional or participial phrases and two Word Study words used accurately; length is on target.
Fewer than two of either, or off the length target.
Two figures named and quoted; the explanation shows how their pictures build one mood.
Figures are named without explanation, or the mood is stated without the pictures that build it.
The origin is accurate and tied to the passage, and the word is reused correctly in a new sentence.
The origin is missing or inaccurate, or the new sentence misuses the word.
Two subordinate clauses and two Word Study words used accurately; length is on target.
Fewer than two of either, or off the length target.

rubrics.title: Quick Write 20 — The Play Inside the Play

ratings.long_description: A clear claim names the layer and what it adds to the play as a whole.
The claim is general, or describes the element without naming a layer.
Two accurate, cited quotations, each explained through its wording.
A quotation is missing, uncited, or left unexplained.
One parallel pair and two Word Study words used accurately; length is on target.
Fewer than two of either, or off the length target.

rubrics.title: Quick Write 21 — Layers in the Verse

criteria.description: Two readings supported by the lines

ratings.long_description: Two distinct readings, each supported by quoted words and explained.
Readings overlap, are unsupported, or quote words without explaining them.

criteria.description: The reading the production will play

ratings.long_description: Chooses one reading, argues for it, and says what the production gives up.
Chooses without a reason, or ignores what is given up.
Two appositives and two Word Study words used accurately; length is on target.
Fewer than two of either, or off the length target.

criteria.description: What the text specifies, and what the choice adds and loses

ratings.long_description: States what the words alone fix, then names one gain and one loss of the staging choice, each specific.
Mixes up text and staging, or names a gain without a loss.
Argues clearly whether the trade is worth it, with a reason tied to the exchange.
States a preference without a reason, or does not decide.
Punctuation sets pauses on purpose and two Word Study words are used accurately; length is on target.
Fewer than two of either, or off the length target.
Six to ten numbered instructions, each one action with a precise verb, in a workable order.
Fewer than six, several actions in one step, or vague verbs.

criteria.description: Delivery plan for pace and pause

ratings.long_description: Names where pace changes and where pauses fall, tied to particular lines.
General advice such as “speak clearly” with no particular lines.
Imperative mood and two Word Study words used accurately; length is on target.
Fewer than two of either, or off the length target.
A clear thesis; layers of meaning and mood are explained; the text and a staged interpretation are compared by what each emphasizes and leaves out.
The thesis is vague, mood or meaning is only asserted, or the comparison is missing.
Quoted lines are accurate, cited by act and scene, and explained through their wording.
Quotations are dropped in, uncited, or left unexplained.
Padding is cut, two Word Study words are used accurately, and the draft is 600 to 900 words.
Wordy passages, fewer than two Word Study words, or off the length target.

rubrics.title: Recitation Q3 — Say It From Memory

ratings.long_description: The whole passage is recited word for word, from memory.
Lines are missing, reordered, or changed, or the passage is clearly read from a script.
Pauses fall where the sense and punctuation call for them, and run-on lines are carried through the line break.
Every line ends with the same drop in the voice, or pauses fall in the middle of a sentence.
Stress, pace, and volume reflect what the passage is doing (a plea, an argument, a reckoning, an accusation).
Delivery is flat or does not change with the sense of the passage.
Audible and clear from start to finish, one continuous take of the passage, and the file or link opens.
Hard to hear in places, cut off, or the file or link does not open.

The essay explains how Shakespeare builds layers of meaning and mood in the scene, shows how the production brings one layer out, and compares the text with a staged interpretation by naming what each emphasizes and what each leaves out.
The analysis describes the scene without explaining layers, the production’s layer is unclear, or the comparison is missing.
Quoted lines are accurate, cited by act and scene, and explained through their wording.
Quotations are inaccurate, uncited, or dropped in without explanation.

The program is organized under clear headings and includes a design page with captioned, credited images, a cast list, and a cited passage; conventions are correct and the PDF export is ready to publish.
Organization is hard to follow, the design page lacks captions or rationales, conventions errors distract, or the export is not publication ready.
A 2 to 3 minute recording gives clear, sequenced instructions for the key moment, with a plan for pace and pause, and the delivery is easy to follow.
The recording is off the time target, the instructions are vague or out of order, or the delivery is hard to follow.
The sentence follows Fitzgerald’s structure, and the scene is 120 to 180 words of concrete, specific detail about a real place.
The structure is not matched, or the scene is vague or argues instead of showing.
Two specific moves are named, and each is located in the writer’s own scene.
Only one move is named, or the moves are named but not located.
Two appositives and two Word Study words are used accurately; each part is on its word count.
Fewer than two of either, or a part is off its word count.

rubrics.title: Quick Write 26 — What the Symbol Carries

ratings.long_description: Two moments are quoted exactly and explained, and the answer shows what the symbol carries and how it shifts or holds.
Only one moment is explained, quotations are loose, or the explanation only retells.
Three questions are clear, focused, and answerable with sources outside the novel.
Questions are too broad, answerable only from the novel, or fewer than three.
Two layered descriptive sentences and two Word Study words are used accurately; length is on target.
Fewer than two of either, or off the length target.
The question is focused, and three real sources in three formats are named and judged for credibility and accuracy.
The question is still broad, a source is missing or unverified, or credibility is asserted without reasons.
Each format’s strength and limit is stated, and a disagreement or match between sources is resolved with reasons.
A strength or limit is missing, or the sources are compared without a ruling.
A parallel series and two Word Study words are used accurately; length is on target.
No parallel series, fewer than two words, or off the length target.

rubrics.title: Quick Write 28 — One Source, One Claim

ratings.long_description: A real source is cited correctly in MLA form, and its key idea is restated faithfully in the writer’s own words.
The citation has errors, the source is not verifiable, or the paraphrase copies wording or drifts from the source.
One clear claim is supported by the source, with a note on the limits of that support, in a formal register.
The claim is unclear, the source does not actually support it, or the tone is casual.
Formal register holds throughout, and two Word Study words are used accurately; length is on target.
Slips in register, fewer than two words, or off the length target.

rubrics.title: Quick Write 29 — Same Promise, Opposite Ends

ratings.long_description: Both writers’ uses of the idea are stated accurately, with the premise and the end each reaches.
One use is misread or unstated, or the passages are summarized without comparison.
One argument is judged more valid, with reasons about its premise and whether its conclusion follows.
The judgment is a reaction (agreement or dislike) without reasons about premise or reasoning.
Two concession sentences and two Word Study words are used accurately; length is on target.
Fewer than two of either, or off the length target.
The thesis is clear, and the strongest counterclaim is stated fairly and in full.
The thesis is vague, or the counterclaim is a strawman or incomplete.
The answer uses evidence, concedes what is true, and shows why the thesis still stands.
The answer dismisses the counterclaim, or offers no evidence.
Two quotations are integrated and punctuated correctly, and two Word Study words are used accurately; length is on target.
Fewer than two of either, quotations dropped in, or off the length target.
All parts of a business letter are present and correct, in a polite, professional tone.
A part of the format is missing or wrong, or the tone is casual.
The three paragraphs make a clear pitch, and the spoken opening is 60 to 90 seconds and revised from feedback.
A paragraph is missing or vague, or the spoken opening is off time or unrevised.
Two transitions and two Word Study words are used accurately; the letter is on length.
Fewer than two of either, or off the length target.
All parts are present and in order, and the argument answers the refined question with a counterclaim answered.
A part is missing or out of order, or the argument is unclear.
Evidence from the novel and at least four credible sources is cited in MLA form, with a correct Works Cited list.
Sources are thin or unverified, or citations and the Works Cited list have errors.
Two Word Study words are used accurately; the draft is 900 to 1,400 words and edited for clarity.
Fewer than two words, or off the length target.

rubrics.title: Recitation Q4 — Say It From Memory

ratings.long_description: The full passage is recited, essentially word for word, from memory.
Part of the passage is missing, out of order, or clearly read rather than recited.
Pauses and stresses follow the sense and the structure of the sentences, and the pace is unhurried.
Pauses are missing or misplaced, or the pace is rushed.
The delivery reflects what the passage is doing, and is not a flat monotone.
The delivery is flat or shows little sense of the passage’s meaning.
Every word is audible, the recording is complete, and it is in a usable format.
Words are hard to hear, the recording is cut off, or the file will not open.

3. Graded items

The Jazz Age Feature (50 pts, Tier 3, 4-criterion rubric).

  • ELA.10.C.1.3 (primary: argue an answer, counterclaim answered, evidence from the novel and sources), C.1.4 (information from multiple sources), C.4.1 (research and discernment, four or more sources, JSTOR, two or more formats), C.5.2 (publication-ready export, multimedia that carries evidence), C.5.1 (part: the Feature may be built in PowerPoint or Sway), C.2.1 (the recorded Premiere), C.3.1 (conventions), R.2.1 (structure and features), EE.1.1, EE.5.1 (MLA).
  • TEKS 10(C), 9(A)-(E), 11(A)-(I), 7(D), 7(F), 8(C), 1(C).
  • Rubric criteria: research and source discernment (14), including sources in more than one format and an account of what each format could and could not establish; argument (14); feature craft and publication quality (12); the Premiere (10).

Recitation Q4 (20 pts). Rubric: accuracy 8, phrasing and pause 4, expression 4, recording quality 4. C.2.1 is partial: a memorized recitation of a public-domain text is delivery practice, not an original presentation with a thesis. R.2.2 and R.2.3 are touched only through the passages chosen (the Gettysburg Address, Douglass, Fitzgerald, Lazarus). R.1.4 applies only if the Lazarus sonnet is chosen. Menu: four passages, device-agnostic recording.

Pitch Discussion (10 pts). FL EE.4.1 (light), C.1.5, C.4.1 (a first narrowing of the question). TEKS 1(A) and 1(D): collaborative participation and building on others' ideas are met. The consensus-building and ground-rule clause of 1(D) is not exercised in Module 4; the Company Rules step lives in Module 3. MS: Comprehension and Collaboration 1.1, 1.3, 1.4 met; 1.2 (rules and group decision) not met here.

Quick Writes 25 to 32 (10 pts each, Writing & Composition). Covered row by row in §2. Each scoring table is 4 / 4 / 2, with the two-point row naming the week's grammar target and two Word Study words (Quick Write 32's two-point row names Word Study words, length, and editing for clarity).

Independent Reading Check Q4 (Week 9). TEKS 3 (self-selected reading). Built separately.

Intro and outro wrappers (ungraded surveys). Framing only; the outro also serves as the year-end reflection.

This file documents the Honors depth delta on the Module 3 project, "The Players' Company." Format follows H_M2_Honors_Overlay_Notes.md. Standards references live only here, never on student pages. This file covers the project overlay (the four Players' Company lessons). The Designer's Table sprints 9-12 are documented with their own sprint pages.

(a) Depth delta on "The Players' Company" (Standard module project)

The Standard project stays the shared deliverable: the Director's Program (Director's Essay, Design Page, cast list, one cited passage) and the recorded Director's Call. Honors builds no second project. The delta is a harder rubric over the same 50 points and the same 4 criteria, plus one added tab in each project lesson.

Criterion (Standard points)Standard barHonors bar (delta)
Analysis of meaning and mood (15)Explains how Shakespeare builds layers of meaning and mood in the chosen scene; includes at least one comparison of the text against a staged interpretation naming what each emphasizes and leaves out.Weighs a comic and a darker reading of the scene and says which the production leans toward and what that costs. Compares two published productions of the same exchange (from reviews or production notes the student actually read), not one staging, and says what the two choices show about what the text leaves open.
Evidence and explanation (12)Quoted lines are accurate, cited by act and scene, and explained through their wording.Adds one scholarly literary source on the play found on JStor, cited in MLA, with one idea paraphrased and used to change or sharpen the director's thesis. Every line cited in the AI critique is checked against the play.
Program craft and publication quality (12)Organized under scannable headings, a Design Page with captions and credits, correct conventions, publication-ready PDF export.Director's Essay runs 900 to 1,200 words (Standard: 700 to 1,000) and carries the second production, the JStor idea, and the AI critique without losing its organization. Works-cited entry for the JStor source is correct MLA.
The Director's Call (11)Clear, sequenced spoken instructions for the key moment; delivery.Instructions reflect the interpretation the essay argues, including the choice made between the comic and darker readings; the call names the pace and pause that carry it.

Keep the rubric at 4 rows and 50 points so it stays gradable at 500:1. The Standard Quick Writes (QW17-QW24) are unchanged and scored on the Standard rubrics; Honors students do all of them.

(b) What each Honors depth tab adds

Each Honors lesson is a copy of its Standard lesson plus one tab, "Honors depth," placed before the last tab. The Quick Write PDF checkpoint that closes the lesson also gathers the depth answers (the lesson-4 draft PDF too), and the whole-lesson PDF gathers them automatically.

LessonWeeksDepth tab adds
players-lesson-1-the-company.html1-2Two readings of the chosen scene's role in a comedy: a comic reading and a darker reading, each tied to one line, and which the production will lean toward and lose. A JStor search plan for the literary source due in Lesson 2: plain and scholarly search terms, filters, and how a result will be judged. Includes the school's shared JStor login wording (reused from H_M1_JStor_Research_Tutorial.html; credentials are not repeated on the page, students are pointed to that lesson).
players-lesson-2-the-reading.html3-4One scholarly literary source on the play: found and verified on JStor, MLA citation, one idea paraphrased with its page, and how it changes the director's thesis (thesis rewritten if it changed). The Week 4 PDF includes these answers; students return to the "Play inside the play" tab to download it after finishing.
players-lesson-3-the-staging.html5-7Two productions of the same exchange (the exchange chosen in the Director's Note), each described from a published review or production notes. The student logs source (title, publication, date, where read), company, and what the choice emphasizes and leaves out, then compares. The lesson gives no web address; students add one if they read the source online (see sourcing note below).
players-lesson-4-opening-night.html8-9AI verify-and-critique: an AI tool drafts a director's note for the scene, and the student pastes prompt and draft, then marks three errors or flattenings with act, scene and line evidence. Plus the honors Director's Essay length (900 to 1,200 words) and a plan for where the second production, the JStor idea, and the AI critique sit. The finished-essay length mentions in the Standard lesson (700 to 1,000) are changed to 900 to 1,200 in the Honors copy. The Quick Write 24 draft range (600 to 900) is unchanged.

(c) Decisions and cautions

  • AI is optional. Per program rule, AI use is awareness, not required. The AI critique tab says so and tells students who would rather not use a tool to ask the teacher for a sample AI draft. Teachers should keep one on hand (any sample note produced by M365 Copilot for a scene will do).
  • Production sourcing. No production-review URLs are cited in the lessons, because none was confirmed. Students locate two published reviews or production notes themselves and log them by title, publication, date, and location of the description. Teachers: accept a review only if the student can show where the description of the exchange appears; an AI-named review the student has not opened does not count. JStor carries theatre-journal reviews of productions; company websites carry production notes.
  • Namespace. Honors copies use the project key eng2h.players (Standard uses eng2.players), as the Honors trial lessons use eng2h.trial, so Standard and Honors answers never collide on a shared device.
  • JStor. The shared login is the Q1 login; see H_M1_JStor_Research_Tutorial.html. Sources must be opened by the student on JStor.

(d) Standards note

  • Standard = the full benchmark set for 1001340 as mapped in M3_teacher_Standards_Map.md.
  • Rigor = depth, not quantity. The overlay adds interpretive demand rather than coverage volume: a second reading of the scene, a second production compared, one scholarly source used to change a claim, and a critique of an AI interpretation against the text. These deepen the Standard coverage of reading the text closely, comparison of a text with a staged interpretation, research and paraphrase, and writing and revision, all mapped in M3_teacher_Standards_Map.md; this file adds no new benchmark rows.
  • The JStor source in Lesson 2 reaches the research and paraphrase expectations more fully than the Standard project does.

(e) Sourcing/verification log

  • No quotation from the play appears in the four depth tabs. The Standard lesson quotations are copied unchanged from the Standard files, which the gate verified against BLD\src\parts\mnd_*.txt.
  • No external URLs were added. The JStor login wording is reused from H_M1_JStor_Research_Tutorial.html (shared school account); the password is not repeated.

This file documents the Honors depth delta on "The Jazz Age Feature" (Standard module project) and the Honors depth tab added to each of the four Jazz Age project lessons. Standards references live only here. Format follows H_M2_Honors_Overlay_Notes.md. The Designer's Table Sprints 13-18 are documented with their own pages.

(a) Depth delta on "The Jazz Age Feature" (50 points, same four criteria)

Honors students complete the same project, the same Quick Writes (QW25-QW32), and the same Premiere. The rubric keeps the Standard criteria and point values. The descriptors are harder, and the graded Feature carries the added requirements below.

Criterion (points)Standard barHonors bar (delta)
Research and source discernment (14)The novel plus at least 4 credible sources, at least 1 from JSTOR, in at least two formats; an account of what each format could and could not establish.The novel plus at least 6 credible sources, at least 2 from JSTOR (one on Fitzgerald or the 1920s, found in the sources lesson), in at least two formats. A written source-format reflection says what each format showed best, what it could not establish, and which source was trusted where two disagreed. The question carries a stated "so what" for its readership and enters two real scholarly conversations.
Argument (14)Claim, counterclaim answered, evidence from the novel and sources.The counterclaim is the strongest version, tested against an AI-written counterargument and answered point by point (where it is strong, where it fails). A third speech or essay is set beside the two compared in QW29, with a judgment of which argument is most valid. The thesis shows what the testing changed.
Feature craft and publication quality (12)Structure, multimedia carrying evidence, conventions, MLA.Length 1,400-1,800 words (Standard 1,000-1,400). Structure holds at the longer length: added words deepen sections, they do not pad. Works Cited lists every source opened, with no invented entries.
The Premiere (10)Organization, perspective, delivery.The recorded Premiere (3-4 minutes) states the question's "so what" in its opening and names the strongest objection and the answer to it.

Total stays 50. The rubric stays at four rows for gradability at 500:1. No separate Honors submission file: the depth-tab answers travel in each lesson's PDF, and the longer Feature goes in the same Module 4 Project submission.

The Week 8 Quick Write 32 draft keeps its Standard length target (900-1,400 words). The Honors length belongs to the final Feature.

(b) What each Honors depth tab adds

Each tab is data-tab="depth", titled "Honors depth," placed before the last tab (Wrap up or Turn in). The answers are saved with the engine and are included in the lesson's PDF.

14 pts		 A clear, committed answer to the refined question; a counterclaim stated fairly and answered; evidence from both the novel and the sources. The claim is unclear, the counterclaim is missing or a strawman, or the evidence comes from only one place. 14
Feature craft & publication quality
12 pts		 Lede, nut graf, sections, and close in order; at least two multimedia elements that carry evidence; clean conventions; an MLA Works Cited; a publication-ready PDF. A structural part is missing, multimedia only decorates, or citations and conventions have errors. 12
The Premiere
10 pts		 Recorded, 3 to 4 minutes, organized, with a clear perspective and steady delivery (pace, pause, volume, eye contact). Off the time target, read flatly from a script, or the thesis is unclear. 10
Total: 50 pts
📁 M365 REMINDER
Draft and revise the Feature in Word, PowerPoint, or Sway in your school M365 account. Name your file LastName_FirstName_JazzAgeFeature_ELA10, save it to Optima → ELA → ELA10 in OneDrive, export it to PDF, and submit the PDF on this assignment.
🎤 YOUR PREMIERE RECORDING
Use whatever device you have available: a phone, a tablet, a computer webcam, or a school-provided recording tool. Video or audio are both accepted. Aim for 3 to 4 minutes. Speak to an audience rather than reading a paper aloud, and look up from your notes often. If your tool saves a file, upload it directly to this Canvas assignment. If your tool gives you a shareable link instead, paste that link into the Canvas text-entry box.
⚠️ WORTH KNOWING · AI AND YOUR FEATURE
An AI tool can draft a feature in seconds. It can also invent sources, quotations, and statistics that do not exist, and it cannot check a claim against the novel. Every source in your Works Cited must be one you opened and read yourself. If you ask an AI tool for help, keep a short note of what you asked and what you checked on your own, and include it with your Feature.

Four options, equal weight
 
Record one. About 3 minutes.
1Oral Book ResponseABOUT 3 MINUTES
Answer these five out loud, in order. Notes in front of you are fine; a script read word for word is not.
›What is the book, and how far did you get?
›Pick one character. What do they want, and what is in the way?
›Describe a moment where that character makes a choice you would not have made. Why did they make it?
›Read one sentence or short passage you marked, and say why that one.
›Who should read this book, and who should skip it?
2Dramatic ReadingABOUT 3 MINUTES
›Choose a passage of roughly 150 to 300 words where a character is under pressure: deciding, arguing, afraid, or hiding something.
›Read it aloud as that character. Decide before you record what they want in this moment, then let your pace, volume and pauses show it.
›Then talk for about a minute: who is this character, what do they want here, and what did you do with your voice to show it? Name one specific choice you made.
3Make the CaseABOUT 3 MINUTES
You are a guest on a books podcast and the host has given you three minutes to make one argument. House rule of the show: you have to take the side most listeners will not.
›Name what you are arguing about, and say where it falls in the book. Pick something people genuinely disagree over: a moral dilemma, a turn nobody saw coming, or a decision a character made that readers still argue about.
›Take the unpopular side and say it in your first sentence. If most readers think the character was right, argue that they were wrong. If nobody could disagree with your claim, it is not an argument yet.
›Give two pieces of evidence from the text: a line, a scene, something a character says or does. Say roughly where each one falls.
›Answer the strongest objection, the one the host would come back at you with. State it fairly first, then answer it.
›Land it. Finish with one sentence a listener would still be turning over after the episode ends.

›Name the exact point where your version branches off, then describe your ending in detail. What happens, who it happens to, and how does it finish?

›Say what your ending costs. Every ending gives something up. Name what is lost by not keeping the one the author wrote.

quizzes.description:
Welcome to Module 3: A Midsummer Night's Dream.

For the next nine weeks you will read Shakespeare's comedy of lovers, fairies, and a company of workmen who put on a play. Athens has a law that can send a daughter to her death for refusing her father's choice. The wood has rulers of its own, and their quarrel spreads into the weather. The module ends with you directing a short scene from the play for a company of your own.

When desire and law collide, what restores order, and is the restoration real or only a dream?

Answer the few questions below before you begin. There are no wrong answers here. This is your starting point, and you will return to the first question at the end of the module to see how your thinking has changed.

questions.text:
Essential question, first answer

In your own words, and before you have read a page: when what people want collides with the rules of their community, what restores order? Does the order that comes back feel real, or only temporary? A few honest sentences are plenty.

Objectives acknowledgment

This module asks you to be able to do the following by its end. Check each to confirm you have read it.

answers.text: Read a verse comedy closely, using its lines as evidence.
Analyze how figurative language builds mood and how a text carries more than one layer of meaning.
Speak verse aloud and give clear spoken directions.
Write for a public reader: a thesis, evidence, and explanation, in a finished and published document.
Complete the module project, The Players' Company.

questions.text:
Predict the ending

Egeus asks the law of Athens to punish his daughter Hermia for refusing his choice of husband. Which do you expect to matter most to how the play ends?

answers.text: Something outside human control, such as magic or chance

discussions.title: Opening Concept: Pitch Your Production
discussions.html:
You are about to direct a short scene from A Midsummer Night's Dream: a company's concept for how one scene will be staged. Before the staging weeks begin, pitch your concept the way a director pitches to a company before the first rehearsal.

Step 0. Company Rules (one or two sentences, early in the week)

This class works as a company. A company runs on working rules: how notes are given, how a disagreement is settled, and what a decision needs before it counts. Propose one Company Rule, or one change to a rule the class set in an earlier module (add one, drop one, or sharpen one). Say briefly what happened, in this class or in the thread so far, that makes you propose it.

If you think the existing rules are working as they stand, say so and name the specific rule that has done the most work. That is a real position and it needs defending like any other.

Other students may second a proposal in a reply. Your teacher will pin the Company Rules the class converges on and adopt at least one proposal by name. Rules a class writes and then revises are rules a class actually keeps.

Step 1. Your opening concept (by mid-week, 150 to 200 words)

  1. The scene. Name the scene (act and scene, and the first and last line of the stretch you will direct).
  2. The interpretation. In one or two sentences, say what your production brings out of the scene: the layer of meaning or mood you will emphasize.
  3. One staging choice. Name one choice (a setting, a gesture, a pause, a cut) and say what it adds that the text alone does not specify, and what it leaves out or downplays.

Step 2. Two replies, each doing a different job (by end of week)

Reply 1 as the Challenger (Devil's Advocate). Pick one classmate. Name the weakest point in their concept and ask one honest question that would force them to defend it. Pressure the concept, not the person.

Reply 2 as the Synthesizer. Read a stretch of the thread, at least four or five posts, and stand back from it. Which kind of choice (setting, gesture, pause, cut) is this company mostly reaching for, and which is it most divided over? Name one concept on the other side of your own that you think is genuinely strong. Then say whether anything you read changed your concept, and if it did not, why the objections did not reach it.

Guidance

  • A concept is a claim about the scene, not a finished program. If your post reads like a finished director's essay, you have written past the pitch.
  • Playing Challenger is not the same as being unkind. Pressure-testing a classmate's choice now saves them from a weak point a reader would catch later.
  • You are not directing anyone else's scene. Every submission stays a solo piece; this discussion only trades feedback before the staging weeks.
  • The Synthesizer reply requires you to name a strong concept different from your own. Doing it here, in public, makes it easier to compare a text with a staging later.
  • "Nothing changed my mind" is an acceptable conclusion. "I did not read anything that might have" is not.

discussions.title: The Feature Pitch: State Your Question
discussions.html:
The Jazz Age Feature is an investigative feature that answers a question the novel raises about the American dream and about what community a self-made person belongs to. A feature begins with a pitch: the question, the angle, and a reason a reader should care. State yours the way a writer pitches an editor.

Step 1. Your pitch (by mid-week, 150 to 200 words)

  1. The question. State the question the feature will answer, narrowed enough that evidence can answer it. A question such as "What is the American dream?" is too broad. A question tied to the novel and to evidence is the target.
  2. The angle. State the answer you currently expect and the reason a reader should care.
  3. The evidence. Name one moment in the novel and at least two kinds of source you expect to use (for example, a scholarly article, an image, a table of numbers, a recording), and say briefly what each could show.

Step 2. Two replies, each doing a different job (by end of week)

Reply 1 as the Challenger. Pick one classmate. Name the weakest point in the pitch, whether the question is too broad, the angle outruns the evidence, or a source cannot show what the pitch needs. Ask one honest question that would force the writer to defend it. Pressure the reasoning, not the person.

Reply 2 as the Synthesizer. Read at least four or five posts and stand back. Which kinds of question is this class mostly asking, and which is it most divided over? Name one idea from another pitch that could strengthen your own. Then say what, if anything, you will change in your own pitch because of what you read, and if nothing, why the objections did not reach it.

Guidance

  • A pitch is a promise to investigate, not a finished argument. If the post reads like a completed feature, it has gone past the pitch.
  • Being the Challenger is not the same as being unkind. A weak question found now saves the writer from a weak feature later.
  • Every feature stays a solo piece. This discussion trades feedback only; no one writes anyone else's feature.
  • A source can only show what its format can show. A table of numbers cannot show motive; a photograph cannot show a trend. Name what each source in the pitch can and cannot do.
  • "Nothing moved me" is an acceptable conclusion. "I did not read anything that might have" is not.
